messages.subject: Comparing and analyzing predicts
parts:
Dear All

I have two question I have not been able to find alone an answer for, so here they go.

My aim with my current project is to argue in favor of MIMIC models when building democracy indices. I have variables that are indicators and variables that are causes of a latent index, as they should. I try to compare this MIMIC model with a regular Latent Model.

1. The MIMIC model fits much much better than the Regular Latent, achieving conventional standards for good fitting. But when I predict factor scores for the two models, the predicted values are almost identical (correlate at 0.999). I wonder why is that so. In my head they should predict scores that were at least somewhat different. But they do not.

2. Is there a way to compute in Lavaan the confidence intervals around the estimated scores for the latent variables?  I only see reference to the confidence intervals around the parameterEstimates, but nothing about the predicted values. lavPredict does not accept the options for CIs present in the regular predict function. Am I missing something in here?

Cheers!
Fernando Bizzarro Neto
University of Notre Dame

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Comparing and analyzing predicts
parts:
Fernando--
     Things to think about--
     1.  Think about how the factor scores reported by lavaan are computed.  The determinate part of a factor score is a prediction of the common factor based on all of the observed variables in the model--not just the ones that load on the factor.  Using the regression method for estimating this number, the formula is similar to that for regression weights--covariances divided by the inverse of the covariance matrix of the predictors (here, all observed variables).  You use all the same observed variables, and they are all still correlated with the factor, so there is much that is similar statistically
     2.  You say that the MIMIC model provides better fit, which I assume means a better chi-square value and derivatives.  But the chi-square value just tells you that there is more information in the data than is accounted for by your model.  That "more" may have nothing to do with this common factor, so it has no effect on the determinate part of the factor scores.
     3.  Remember that this is only the determinate part of the score.  There is also an indeterminate part.  This part could be very different across models.  The fewer indicators loading on the factor, the greater the indeterminacy--though using fewer indicators may lead to stronger loadings, which will offset that effect.
--Ed Rigdon

Guttman, L. (1955). The determinacy of factor score matrices with implications for five other basic problems of common-factor theory. The British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8, 65-81.

Schönemann, P.H., & Steiger, J.H. (1976). Regression component analysis. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 29, 175-189.
